title: Renovation Permits for Investors: What Needs One
metaDescription: Which rehab work usually needs a permit, why skipping permits hurts appraisals, buyer inspections and insurance, and how inspections fit a rehab schedule.
h1: Renovation Permits for Investors: What Usually Needs One and Why It Matters at Exit
dek: Most structural, electrical, plumbing, mechanical and roofing work on an investor rehab needs a permit, while purely cosmetic work usually does not. Skipping permits rarely saves time in the end: unpermitted work surfaces at appraisal, during buyer inspections and in insurance claims, and inspections can be scheduled into the rehab like any other trade.
keyTakeaways: Rules are local, but structural changes, new or altered electrical, plumbing and HVAC, roofing and most additions typically require permits.
Paint, flooring, cabinets and countertops in the same footprint, and fixture swaps on existing connections are commonly exempt, but check local rules first.
Unpermitted work tends to surface at exit: appraisers, buyer inspectors, title searches, lenders and insurers all have ways of finding it.
Rough-in and final inspections are schedule milestones, so plan trade sequencing around them instead of treating them as interruptions.
Pull permit history before you buy, because open or expired permits and prior unpermitted work become your problem at closing.

sections.h2: Why do permit rules vary so much from place to place?
sections.body:
Building permits are issued by local jurisdictions: a city building department, a county development services office, or in some smaller towns a township or a state agency acting on their behalf. Most adopt a version of the model codes published by the International Code Council, such as the International Residential Code for one- and two-family homes, but they adopt different editions, amend them, and set their own rules about what work is exempt from permits.

That is why the same kitchen remodel can need one combined permit in one suburb and separate building, electrical and plumbing permits in the next. Some cities require licensed trade contractors to pull their own trade permits. Some allow an owner to pull permits for a property they own; many restrict that privilege for investment or rental property. Some jurisdictions have historic districts where exterior changes need design review before a building permit is even considered.

For an investor working in more than one market, the takeaway is simple: never assume the rules from your last project apply to the next one. Before you finalize scope, check the jurisdiction's permit exemption list, which is usually published on the building department's website, and confirm who is allowed to pull each permit. A contractor who works that jurisdiction regularly should be able to answer both questions without looking them up.

The rest of this guide describes typical patterns. Treat them as a starting point for that local check, not a substitute for it.

sections.h2: What work typically needs a permit?
sections.body:
Across most jurisdictions, the following categories of work commonly require a permit on a residential rehab:
- Structural work: removing or altering load-bearing walls, adding or enlarging openings for doors and windows, beam replacement, foundation repair, and new or rebuilt decks and porches above a certain height
- Electrical work beyond like-for-like device replacement: new circuits, panel or service changes, rewiring, adding outlets or fixtures on new runs, and generator or EV charger connections
- Plumbing work beyond fixture replacement: moving or adding fixtures, replacing supply or drain lines, water heater replacement in many places, and sewer lateral repair or replacement
- Mechanical work: furnace, boiler, air conditioner and heat pump replacement, new ductwork, and gas line changes
- Roofing: full re-roofs and often significant repairs, especially where sheathing is replaced
- Additions, finished basements and attic conversions that create habitable space
- Changes to the number of dwelling units, such as converting a single-family house to a duplex or legalizing a basement apartment
- Window replacement where the opening size changes, and in some jurisdictions any window replacement because of energy code or egress requirements
- Demolition of structures, and sometimes interior demolition beyond a certain extent

If a job involves fire separation between units, egress windows in sleeping rooms, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, or anything a future inspector would test, expect a permit to be involved somewhere. The common thread is life safety: work that affects structure, fire, electrical shock, gas, sanitation or escape routes is what code officials want to see.

sections.h2: What work usually does not need a permit?
sections.body:
Cosmetic and like-for-like replacement work is commonly exempt, though again, exemption lists differ. Typical examples include:
- Interior and exterior painting
- Flooring replacement over an existing, sound subfloor
- Cabinet and countertop replacement in the same layout, without moving plumbing or adding circuits
- Replacing faucets, toilets and sinks on existing supply and drain connections
- Replacing light fixtures, switches and receptacles on existing circuits
- Trim, doors within existing openings, and hardware
- Minor drywall patching
- Gutters, and in some places fencing and small sheds under a size limit

The trap is scope creep. A cabinet swap becomes a layout change, the sink moves to the island, the range moves to the other wall, and suddenly there is new plumbing, new circuits and possibly a gas line. Each of those changes can bring a permit requirement that was not part of the original plan.

Another trap is cumulative work. Some jurisdictions require a permit once the overall project crosses a size or value threshold, even if each piece would be exempt alone. Others require permits for work in certain property types, such as rentals or multifamily buildings, that would be exempt in an owner-occupied house.

When in doubt, call the building department and ask. The answer costs nothing, and having it in writing or noted in your project file helps if the question comes up later.

sections.h2: How does unpermitted work hurt your exit?
sections.body:
The usual argument for skipping permits is speed and cost. The usual result is that the bill arrives at exit, when you have the least leverage.

Appraisals are the first exposure. Appraisers note additions, finished basements, extra bedrooms and bathrooms, and some check public records for square footage and room counts. If the record shows a two-bedroom house and you are selling a three-bedroom with a finished basement, the appraiser may not give full value to the unpermitted space, or may note it as a condition the lender has to address. On a BRRRR refinance, that can directly reduce the loan amount.

Buyer inspections are the second. Experienced home inspectors recognize new work: a new panel with no inspection sticker, new plumbing in an old house, fresh framing in the basement. Many buyers' agents now pull permit history as a matter of routine. Unpermitted work becomes a negotiation item, a request to permit and inspect before closing, or a reason for a buyer to walk.

Title and municipal checks are the third. Some cities require a pre-sale inspection or a certificate of occupancy for transfers or rentals, and open or missing permits can block that process.

Insurance is the fourth. If a fire starts in unpermitted wiring or water damage traces to unpermitted plumbing, an insurer may scrutinize the claim. Coverage outcomes depend on the policy and circumstances, but you do not want to be arguing about it.

Retroactive permitting is possible in many places, but it can require opening finished walls so an inspector can see the work. That is slower and more expensive than doing it right the first time.

sections.h2: How do inspections fit into a rehab schedule?
sections.body:
Inspections are milestones, and a good schedule is built around them. The typical sequence on a rehab with structural and systems work looks like this:
- Footing or foundation inspection, if there is new foundation work, before concrete is placed
- Framing inspection after structural changes are complete, often combined with or following the rough trade inspections
- Rough electrical, rough plumbing and rough mechanical inspections after the systems are run but before walls are closed
- Insulation inspection in jurisdictions that require one, after insulation is installed and before drywall
- Final inspections for each trade and the building permit once work is complete

The critical rule is that walls do not close until rough inspections pass. That single dependency drives a lot of rehab sequencing. Drywall crews cannot be scheduled firmly until rough inspections are passed, and if an inspection fails, corrections and a re-inspection come before drywall.

To keep inspections from becoming delays:
- Know how the jurisdiction schedules inspections, whether online, by phone, or by request through the permit holder, and how much lead time it typically needs
- Coordinate trades so rough-ins finish together and inspections can be requested as a group where allowed
- Have the permit card, approved plans and any required documents on site and accessible
- Make sure the site is open and safe for the inspector, with clear access to the work
- Walk the work before requesting inspection so obvious items are caught internally

Treat a failed inspection as information. It tells you exactly what needs to be fixed while the fix is still cheap.

sections.h2: What should you check about permits before you buy?
sections.body:
Permit due diligence belongs in your offer analysis, not your rehab kickoff. A few checks can change your numbers.

Pull the permit history for the address from the building department, usually online. Look for open permits that were never finaled and expired permits on work that appears complete. Either one can become your obligation once you own the property, and some jurisdictions will not issue new permits until old ones are closed out.

Compare what you see in the house to what the records show. An addition, finished basement, converted garage, extra bathroom or added unit with no permit history is a red flag. You may need to permit it, rebuild it, remove it, or value the property without it.

Check for code enforcement cases, violations and liens. Distressed and bank-owned properties often carry open code cases for vacancy, exterior condition or unsafe structures. Those cases do not disappear at transfer.

Check zoning and unit count if you are buying small multifamily. A building being used as a duplex may be zoned or permitted as a single-family house, which affects both legal use and financing.

Finally, ask whether the jurisdiction requires a vacant-building registration, rental registration, or point-of-sale inspection. These programs add steps and sometimes required repairs.

sections.h2: Who should pull the permits on an investor project?
sections.body:
In most cases, the contractor performing the work should pull the permits for that work. There are several reasons.

Many jurisdictions require licensed trade contractors to pull electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits themselves. Owner-builder permits, where allowed, often come with restrictions on rental or resale property, and some require the owner to sign an affidavit that they will live in the house or will not sell for a period of time. Investors who pull owner permits to save money may be making representations that do not match their plans.

When the contractor pulls the permit, the contractor is the responsible party in the building department's records. Inspection failures, corrections and code questions go to the people who can fix them. That also keeps the inspector's conversation with the person who did the work.

On a project with a general contractor coordinating multiple trades, the general typically pulls the building permit and the licensed trades pull their own trade permits, or the general pulls them if the jurisdiction allows. The general should track all of them and confirm finals before final billing.

As the owner, ask to see each permit, keep copies in your property file, and confirm finals at the end. A finaled permit is a document you will use at sale, at refinance and with your insurer. Genstone handles permits and inspections as part of the projects it manages, and the closed-out permits go into the project documentation with lien waivers and photos.

sections.h2: Do permits slow a rehab down?
sections.body:
Permits add steps, but the delay is usually less than investors expect and far less than the cost of unpermitted work coming back later.

The time cost has two parts. The first is plan review and permit issuance. For simple trade permits, many jurisdictions issue over the counter or online with little review. Structural changes, additions, unit conversions and work in historic districts may need drawings and a review period that varies widely by jurisdiction and season. The second is inspection scheduling, which depends on inspector availability.

You can reduce both:
- Identify permit-requiring work during scope development, not after demolition
- Submit permit applications as early as the jurisdiction allows, ideally so issuance lines up with demolition finishing
- Separate work that needs drawings from work that does not, so simple permits are not held up by complex ones
- Start non-permit work, such as cosmetic demolition, cleanout and exterior cleanup, while waiting where that is allowed
- Use contractors who know the local inspectors' expectations, which cuts down on failed inspections

The schedule risk to watch is the late-discovered permit: a wall you planned to patch turns out to need structural repair, or the old panel cannot be reused. That is where contingency planning matters. A scope with a realistic contingency and a contractor who flags permit implications immediately keeps those discoveries from turning into a stalled job.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace a water heater?
faqs.a: In many jurisdictions, yes. Water heater replacement often requires a plumbing permit, and a mechanical or gas permit if it is gas-fired, because of venting, gas connections and temperature and pressure relief valve requirements. Some places exempt like-for-like electric water heater swaps. Because the rules vary and the safety stakes are real, check the local building department's exemption list or ask the plumber, who should know the local requirement and pull the permit if one is needed.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with unpermitted work?
faqs.a: Often you can, but it usually costs you. Depending on the state, sellers may have to disclose known unpermitted work, and buyers, lenders and appraisers may discount it, require permitting before closing, or walk away. Cash buyers may accept it with a price reduction. If the unpermitted work affects safety, such as wiring, gas or structure, the issue is larger than price. Retroactively permitting the work before listing is often the cleaner path.

faqs.q: What happens if a permit inspection fails?
faqs.a: The inspector notes the items that do not meet code, the contractor corrects them, and a re-inspection is scheduled. Some jurisdictions charge a re-inspection fee. Failed inspections are common and not usually a disaster if the corrections are minor. The real cost is schedule: walls cannot close until rough inspections pass, so a failure can idle drywall and finish trades. Pre-walking the work before requesting inspection catches most avoidable failures.

faqs.q: Can an investor pull an owner-builder permit on a flip?
faqs.a: It depends on the jurisdiction. Some allow owner-builder permits only for an owner-occupied primary residence. Others allow them more broadly but require the owner to perform or directly supervise the work, and some restrict selling the property for a period afterward. Licensed trade work such as electrical and plumbing is often excluded. Read the owner-builder affidavit carefully before signing, because signing one for a flip you plan to sell immediately may be a misrepresentation.

faqs.q: Does cosmetic work ever need a permit?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Historic districts may require approval for exterior paint colors, windows, doors and roofing materials. Some jurisdictions require permits for any work in multifamily buildings or rentals. Others trigger permits based on project value or size. And cosmetic projects that drift into layout changes, new circuits or moved plumbing pick up permit requirements along the way. Confirm the local exemption list before assuming a cosmetic scope is permit-free.
